claim: Latrophilins are postsynaptic adhesion-GPCRs that engage in trans-synaptic complexes with presynaptic teneurins and FLRTs.
source: Latrophilins are postsynaptic adhesion-GPCRs that engage in trans-synaptic complexes with presynaptic teneurins and FLRTs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work throughout the manuscript.

claim: In mouse CA1-region neurons, Latrophilin-2 and Latrophilin-3 are essential for formation of entorhinal-cortex-derived and Schaffer-collateral-derived synapses, respectively.
source: In mouse CA1-region neurons, Latrophilin-2 and Latrophilin-3 are essential for formation of entorhinal-cortex-derived and Schaffer-collateral-derived synapses, respectively.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by prior published work (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019) as cited in the introduction.

claim: Latrophilin-2 and Latrophilin-3 exhibit constitutive GPCR activity that increases cAMP levels.
source: Here, we show that Latrophilin-2 and Latrophilin-3 exhibit constitutive GPCR activity that increases cAMP levels, which was blocked by a mutation interfering with G-protein and arrestin interactions of GPCRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2, where expression of WT Lphn2 and Lphn3 in HEK293T cells caused constitutive elevation of pink Flamindo fluorescence (cAMP indicator) and PKA activity.

claim: The T4L mutation blocks the GPCR activity of Latrophilin-2 and Latrophilin-3.
source: Here, we show that Latrophilin-2 and Latrophilin-3 exhibit constitutive GPCR activity that increases cAMP levels, which was blocked by a mutation interfering with G-protein and arrestin interactions of GPCRs.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2A and 2D showing that the T4L mutation completely abolished the specific pink Flamindo signal and PKA-indicator signal induced by Lphn2 and Lphn3.

claim: The T4L mutation impaired the ability of Latrophilin-2 and Latrophilin-3 to rescue the synapse-loss phenotype in Latrophilin-2 and Latrophilin-3 knockout neurons in vivo.
source: The same mutation impaired the ability of Latrophilin-2 and Latrophilin-3 to rescue the synapse-loss phenotype in Latrophilin-2 and Latrophilin-3 knockout neurons in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data in Figures 4 and 5 showing that T4L-mutant Lphn2 and Lphn3 failed to rescue synaptic connectivity deficits in conditional knockout neurons, and by rabies tracing data in Figure 6.

claim: Latrophilin-2 and Latrophilin-3 require GPCR signaling in synapse formation.
source: Our results suggest that Latrophilin-2 and Latrophilin-3 require GPCR signaling in synapse formation, indicating that latrophilins promote synapse formation in the hippocampus by activating a classical GPCR-signaling pathway.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined evidence that latrophilins exhibit GPCR activity (Figure 2) and that blocking this activity with the T4L mutation prevents rescue of synapse formation deficits (Figures 3-6).

claim: Few proteins are known to be essential for synapse formation in vertebrates or invertebrates.
source: Few proteins are known to be essential for synapse formation in vertebrates or invertebrates.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by the review of literature in the introduction.

claim: Nearly all candidate synaptic adhesion molecules tested by rigorous genetic approaches are not required for synapse formation per se.
source: However, nearly all the candidate synaptic adhesion molecules that have been tested by rigorous genetic approaches are not required for synapse formation per se.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Shen et al., 2004; Duan et al., 2018; Missler et al., 2003; Nair et al., 2013; Varoqueaux et al., 2006) discussed in the introduction.

claim: Some candidate synaptic adhesion molecules direct neuronal processes to the correct position of future synapses.
source: Instead, some of these candidate synaptic adhesion molecules, such as SYG1 in Caenorhabditis elegans (Shen et al., 2004) or cadherins in the retina (Duan et al., 2018), direct neuronal processes to the correct position of future synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies on SYG1 and cadherins.

claim: Other candidate synaptic adhesion molecules specify the properties of synapses.
source: Other candidate synaptic adhesion molecules, such as neurexins and their ligands (reviewed in Südhof, 2018) or the SALM/Lrfn family (reviewed in Lie et al., 2018), specify the properties of synapses (Missler et al., 2003; Nair et al., 2013; Varoqueaux et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews and specific studies on neurexins and SALM/Lrfn proteins.

claim: Deletion of cerebellin-1 or GluD2 causes robust parallel-fiber synapse loss in the cerebellum, but synapses are only eliminated secondarily after they were established.
source: Although deletion of cerebellin-1 or GluD2 causes robust parallel-fiber synapse loss in the cerebellum, synapses are only eliminated secondarily after they were established.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by a citation to a review (Yuzaki, 2018).

claim: Only a fraction of parallel-fiber synapses is lost after cerebellin-1 or GluD2 deletion, whereas all parallel-fiber synapses exhibit altered synaptic plasticity.
source: Moreover, only a fraction of parallel-fiber synapses is lost, whereas all parallel-fiber synapses exhibit altered synaptic plasticity (reviewed in Yuzaki, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Cerebellin-1 and -2 deletions do not hinder initial synapse formation in other parts of the brain, but impair synapse function and lead to secondary synapse elimination.
source: In other parts of the brain, cerebellin-1 and −2 deletions also do not hinder initial synapse formation, but impair synapse function and also lead to secondary synapse elimination (Rong et al., 2012; Seigneur and Südhof, 2018; Seigneur et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Latrophilins and BAIs are adhesion-GPCRs that are essential for establishing synapses in all brain regions in which they have been tested.
source: Among these molecules are two families of adhesion-GPCRs, latrophilins and BAIs, that are essential for establishing synapses in all brain regions in which they have been tested (Kakegawa et al., 2015; Sigoillot et al., 2015; Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Adhesion-GPCRs characteristically contain large extracellular sequences with multiple potential ligand-binding domains and a canonical GAIN domain that is coupled to the seven-transmembrane region module characteristic of GPCRs.
source: Adhesion-GPCRs characteristically contain large extracellular sequences with multiple potential ligand-binding domains and a canonical GAIN domain that is coupled to the seven-transmembrane region module characteristic of GPCRs (reviewed in Vizurraga et al., 2020; Morgan et al., 2019; Folts et al., 2019; Purcell and Hall, 2018).
evidence: This is a general statement about adhesion-GPCRs supported by citations to reviews.

claim: Most adhesion-GPCRs have a long cytoplasmic region.
source: Most adhesion-GPCRs additionally have a long cytoplasmic region.
evidence: This is a general statement about adhesion-GPCRs based on established knowledge.

claim: The three mammalian latrophilins (Lphn1-3) feature N-terminal lectin- and olfactomedin-like ligand-binding domains, a serine-threonine rich and 'hormone binding' domain of unknown function, and a canonical GAIN domain.
source: The three mammalian latrophilins (Lphn1-3) follow the same design principle as other adhesion-GPCRs. They feature N-terminal lectin- and olfactomedin-like ligand-binding domains, a serine-threonine rich and 'hormone binding' domain of unknown function, and a canonical GAIN domain (Figure 1A; Sugita et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1A showing the domain structure and by a citation to Sugita et al., 1998.

claim: Latrophilin domains are attached to a classical seven-transmembrane region GPCR module, followed by a long cytoplasmic region that interacts at the C-terminus with the PDZ-domain of SHANKs.
source: These domains are attached to a classical seven-transmembrane region GPCR module, followed by a long cytoplasmic region that interacts at the C-terminus with the PDZ-domain of SHANKs (Kreienkamp et al., 2000; Tobaben et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing the interaction with SHANKs.

claim: The N-terminal lectin- and olfactomedin-like domains of latrophilins engage in transcellular interactions with multiple presynaptic ligands, including teneurins and FLRTs.
source: The N-terminal lectin- and olfactomedin-like domains of latrophilins engage in transcellular interactions with multiple presynaptic ligands, including teneurins and FLRTs (Sugita et al., 1998; O'Sullivan et al., 2012; Silva et al., 2011; Boucard et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Multiple latrophilin isoforms are generally co-expressed in the same neurons.
source: Multiple latrophilin isoforms are generally co-expressed in the same neurons.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge.

claim: CA1 pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus co-express Lphn2 and Lphn3 that are targeted to distinct dendritic domains of the same neuron and are essential for formation of different excitatory synaptic inputs.
source: CA1 pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus co-express Lphn2 and Lphn3 that are targeted to distinct dendritic domains of the same neuron and are essential for formation of different excitatory synaptic inputs (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Lphn2 and Lphn3 are redundantly required in the cerebellum for parallel-fiber synapse formation.
source: Moreover, Lphn2 and Lphn3 are redundantly required in the cerebellum for parallel-fiber synapse formation (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: The function of postsynaptic Lphn3 in hippocampal synapse formation requires intact binding sites for both presynaptic teneurins and FLRTs.
source: The function of postsynaptic Lphn3 in hippocampal synapse formation requires intact binding sites for both presynaptic teneurins and FLRTs, indicating that latrophilins may mediate synapse specificity by acting as coincidence detectors that respond to two input signals (Sando et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sando et al., 2019.

claim: Latrophilins may mediate synapse specificity by acting as coincidence detectors that respond to two input signals.
source: The function of postsynaptic Lphn3 in hippocampal synapse formation requires intact binding sites for both presynaptic teneurins and FLRTs, indicating that latrophilins may mediate synapse specificity by acting as coincidence detectors that respond to two input signals (Sando et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the requirement for both ligands, as indicated by the word 'indicating'.

claim: The Lphn2 and Lphn3 mutations do not impair their surface transport and extracellular ligand interactions.
source: Viewed together, these results show that the various Lphn2 and Lphn3 mutations do not impair their surface transport and extracellular ligand interactions.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B-D showing that mutant proteins are expressed on the cell surface and mediate trans-cellular adhesion.

claim: All mutant Lphn2 and Lphn3 proteins were as well expressed on the surface as WT proteins in neurons.
source: Quantifications documented that all mutant proteins were as well expressed on the surface as WT proteins (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The levels of the GPI-anchored Lphn3-ECD protein were slightly lower on the cell surface than those of the other proteins.
source: Only the levels of the GPI-anchored Lphn3-ECD protein were slightly lower on the cell surface than those of the other proteins (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification data in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The fixation procedure used produces minor membrane permeability and exposure of intracellular antigens.
source: Cell fixation with 4% PFA/4% sucrose/PBS alone produced minor membrane permeability and exposure of intracellular antigens.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B where permeabilization with Triton X-100 exposed substantial Homer1 signal, suggesting that fixation alone generates minor permeability.

claim: The T4L mutation and co-expression of the cAMP-specific phosphodiesterase PDE7b prevent cAMP increases by Lphn2 or Lphn3.
source: The T4L mutation and co-expression of the cAMP-specific phosphodiesterase PDE7b prevent cAMP increases by Lphn2 or Lphn3.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A where both T4L mutation and PDE7b co-expression blocked the Pink Flamindo signal increase.

claim: Without latrophilins, PDE7b had no effect on pink Flamindo fluorescence, suggesting that the observed signal represents background and that the basal levels of cAMP in HEK293T cells are undetectably low at these acquisition settings.
source: Imaging revealed that without latrophilins, PDE7b had no effect on pink Flamindo fluorescence, suggesting that the observed signal represents background and that the basal levels of cAMP in HEK293T cells are undetectably low at these acquisition settings (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A control conditions.

claim: Expression of WT Lphn2 and Lphn3 caused a constitutive elevation of pink Flamindo fluorescence that was blocked by PDE7b, demonstrating that the pink Flamindo signal is specific for cAMP.
source: Expression of WT Lphn2 and Lphn3 caused a constitutive elevation of pink Flamindo fluorescence. This fluorescence increase was blocked by PDE7b, demonstrating that the pink Flamindo signal is specific for cAMP and that Lphn2 and Lphn3 increase cAMP levels (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A with quantification of the Pink Flamindo signal.

claim: The T4L mutation completely abolished the specific pink Flamindo signal, suggesting that it blocks the GPCR activity of Lphn2 and Lphn3.
source: The T4L mutation completely abolished the specific pink Flamindo signal, suggesting that it blocks the GPCR activity of Lphn2 and Lphn3 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A where T4L mutants showed no increase in Pink Flamindo signal.

claim: Co-expression of the PKA indicator with Gαs and various Lphn2 and Lphn3 proteins confirmed that Lphn2 and Lphn3 both activate cAMP signaling.
source: We then used the newly constructed PKA-indicator to examine the effect of WT and mutant Lphn2 and Lphn3 proteins on PKA activity. Co-expression of the PKA indicator with Gαs and various Lphn2 and Lphn3 proteins, without or with PDE7b, confirmed that Lphn2 and Lphn3 both activate cAMP signaling (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D with quantification of phospho-PKA signal.

claim: The Lphn2- and Lphn3-induced PKA-indicator signal was greatly attenuated by PDE7b, confirming that it is due to cAMP.
source: The Lphn2- and Lphn3-induced PKA-indicator signal was greatly attenuated by PDE7b, confirming that it is due to cAMP.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D where PDE7b co-expression reduced the phospho-PKA signal.

claim: The T4L-mutations of Lphn2 and Lphn3 suppressed the PKA-indicator signal induced by Lphn2 or Lphn3, and PDE7b had no additional effect.
source: The T4L-mutations of Lphn2 and Lphn3 similarly suppressed the PKA-indicator signal induced by Lphn2 or Lphn3, and PDE7b had no additional effect (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D where T4L mutants showed reduced phospho-PKA signal similar to PDE7b conditions.

claim: Lphn2 and Lphn3 stimulate cAMP production in cells in a manner dependent on a GPCR transduction mechanism.
source: Together, these data suggest that Lphn2 and Lphn3 stimulate cAMP production in cells in a manner dependent on a GPCR transduction mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data in Figure 2 showing cAMP and PKA activation by latrophilins that is blocked by the T4L mutation.

claim: The Lphn3 deletion robustly decreased (~40%) the excitatory synapse density in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: As shown previously (Sando et al., 2019), the Lphn3 deletion robustly decreased (~40%) the excitatory synapse density in cultured hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A with immunolabeling for vGluT1 and PSD-95 and quantification of synapse density.

claim: The decrease in excitatory synapse density caused by Lphn3 deletion was fully rescued by WT Lphn3 but not by any of the three Lphn3 mutants (Lphn3-ECD, Lphn3-T4L, and Lphn3-ΔCt).
source: This decrease was fully rescued by WT Lphn3 but not by any of the three Lphn3 mutants (Lphn3-ECD, Lphn3-T4L, and Lphn3-ΔCt) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A with quantification of synapse density across different rescue conditions.

claim: Lphn3 functions as a GPCR in synapse formation and this function depends additionally on the cytoplasmic sequences of Lphn3.
source: This result suggests that Lphn3 functions as a GPCR in synapse formation and that this function depends additionally on the cytoplasmic sequences of Lphn3.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that both the T4L mutation (blocking GPCR signaling) and the ΔCt mutation (deleting cytoplasmic sequences) prevent rescue of the synapse density phenotype.

claim: The Lphn3 deletion caused a ~40% decrease in mEPSC frequency, which corroborates the decrease in synapse density.
source: The Lphn3 deletion caused a ~40% decrease in mEPSC frequency, which corroborates the decrease in synapse density, but had only minor effects on the mEPSC amplitude (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B-D with representative traces and quantification of mEPSC frequency and amplitude.

claim: The decrease in mEPSC frequency caused by Lphn3 deletion was fully rescued by WT Lphn3 but not by the three Lphn3 mutants tested.
source: Again, this phenotype was fully rescued by WT Lphn3 but not by the three Lphn3 mutants tested, which were inactive even though they were fully transported to the surface of dendritic spines (Figures 1, 3C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and D with quantification of mEPSC frequency across different rescue conditions.

claim: Lphn3 functions as a GPCR in synapse formation in cultured neurons, and this function additionally requires their long cytoplasmic tail region.
source: These results suggest that Lphn3 functions as a GPCR in synapse formation in cultured neurons, and that this function additionally requires their long cytoplasmic tail region.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined synapse density and mEPSC data showing that both GPCR signaling and cytoplasmic sequences are required for Lphn3 function.

claim: The Lphn2 deletion selectively impaired entorhinal cortical synaptic inputs but not Schaffer-collateral synaptic inputs.
source: The Lphn2 deletion selectively impaired entorhinal cortical synaptic inputs but not Schaffer-collateral synaptic inputs, confirming previous conclusions (Anderson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 with electrophysiological recordings showing reduced perforant path responses but normal Schaffer collateral responses in Lphn2 KO neurons.

claim: The impairment of entorhinal cortical synaptic inputs caused by Lphn2 deletion was rescued by WT but not by T4L-mutant Lphn2.
source: This phenotype was rescued by WT but not by T4L-mutant Lphn2 that is unable to mediate GPCR signaling (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D-F with input-output curves and quantification showing that WT Lphn2 but not T4L-mutant Lphn2 rescues the deficit.

claim: The Lphn3 deletion selectively impaired Schaffer collateral- but not entorhinal cortex-derived synaptic inputs.
source: The Lphn3 deletion, conversely, selectively impaired Schaffer collateral- but not entorhinal cortex-derived synaptic inputs, again confirming previous findings (Sando et al., 2019).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 with electrophysiological recordings showing reduced Schaffer collateral responses but normal perforant path responses in Lphn3 KO neurons.

claim: The impairment of Schaffer collateral synaptic inputs caused by Lphn3 deletion was rescued by WT but not by T4L-mutant Lphn3.
source: This phenotype was also rescued by WT but not by T4L-mutant Lphn3 (Figure 5), confirming that GPCR signaling is essential for latrophilin function in synapse formation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A-C with input-output curves and quantification showing that WT Lphn3 but not T4L-mutant Lphn3 rescues the deficit.

claim: GPCR signaling is essential for latrophilin function in synapse formation.
source: This phenotype was also rescued by WT but not by T4L-mutant Lphn3 (Figure 5), confirming that GPCR signaling is essential for latrophilin function in synapse formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo rescue experiments showing that blocking GPCR signaling with the T4L mutation prevents rescue of synaptic connectivity deficits.

claim: The Lphn3 conditional KO impaired synaptic connectivity as measured by retrograde rabies tracing.
source: Again, the Lphn3 conditional KO impaired synaptic connectivity (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and C with representative images and quantification of rabies-labeled presynaptic neurons.

claim: The impairment of synaptic connectivity caused by Lphn3 conditional KO was rescued by expression of WT Lphn3, but not by the T4L-mutant Lphn3.
source: This phenotype of rescued by expression of WT Lphn3, but not by the T4L-mutant Lphn3 unable to mediate GPCR signaling (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C with quantification of connected neurons showing that WT Lphn3 but not T4L-mutant Lphn3 rescues the deficit.

claim: Latrophilins function as postsynaptic GPCRs that control input-specific excitatory synapse formation in the hippocampus via a GPCR-dependent mechanism.
source: Viewed together, these data indicate that latrophilins function as postsynaptic GPCRs that control input-specific excitatory synapse formation in the hippocampus via a GPCR-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, drawn from the combined evidence that latrophilins exhibit GPCR activity and that this activity is required for their function in synapse formation both in vitro and in vivo.

claim: Lphn2 and Lphn3 are constitutively active GPCRs that enhance cAMP levels when expressed in HEK293 cells.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Lphn2 and Lphn3 are constitutively active GPCRs that enhance cAMP levels when expressed in HEK293 cells, and that the GPCR activity of Lphn2 and Lphn3 is essential for their ability to promote synapse formation in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the main findings, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The GPCR activity of Lphn2 and Lphn3 is essential for their ability to promote synapse formation in vivo.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Lphn2 and Lphn3 are constitutively active GPCRs that enhance cAMP levels when expressed in HEK293 cells, and that the GPCR activity of Lphn2 and Lphn3 is essential for their ability to promote synapse formation in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the main findings, supported by data in Figures 4-6.

claim: Lphn3 requires its cytoplasmic sequences for supporting synapse formation.
source: In addition, we show that Lphn3 requires its cytoplasmic sequences for supporting synapse formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings, supported by data in Figure 3 showing that the Lphn3-ΔCt mutant fails to rescue the synapse formation deficit.

claim: Latrophilins act in synapse formation by transmitting a GPCR-mediated signal, possibly by elevating cAMP.
source: Based on these findings, we propose that latrophilins act in synapse formation by transmitting a GPCR-mediated signal, possibly by elevating cAMP.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the combined findings that latrophilins increase cAMP and require GPCR signaling for synapse formation.

claim: The latrophilin GPCR signal is likely translated into specific organizational activities during synapse formation in a context-dependent manner.
source: Thus, the latrophilin GPCR signal most likely is translated into specific organizational activities during synapse formation in a context- dependent manner, either via interactions of latrophilins with postsynaptic proteins such as SHANKs that are mediated by their cytoplasmic sequences, or via parallel signals induced by other trans-synaptic adhesion complexes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how latrophilin GPCR signaling might achieve specificity in synapse formation.

claim: Analysis of WT and mutant Lphn2 and Lphn3 in HEK293 cells demonstrated that WT Lphn2 and Lphn3 exhibit constitutively active GPCR activity that elevates cAMP levels, and that this activity is blocked by the T4L mutation.
source: First, analysis of WT and mutant Lphn2 and Lphn3 in HEK293 cells demonstrated that WT Lphn2 and Lphn3 exhibit constitutively active GPCR activity that elevates cAMP levels, and that this activity is blocked by the T4L mutation, which is known to abolish GPCR signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of evidence supporting the main conclusion, referring to data in Figure 2.

claim: Analysis of cultured neurons demonstrated that the Lphn2 and Lphn3 mutations do not impair surface transport of Lphn2 and Lphn3 or targeting to dendritic spines.
source: Second, analysis of cultured neurons demonstrated that the Lphn2 and Lphn3 mutations do not impair surface transport of Lphn2 and Lphn3 or targeting to dendritic spines, but that the Lphn3 mutations abolish its ability to rescue the decrease in synapse formation induced by conditional KO of Lphn3.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of evidence, referring to data in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: The Lphn3 mutations abolish its ability to rescue the decrease in synapse formation induced by conditional KO of Lphn3 in cultured neurons.
source: Second, analysis of cultured neurons demonstrated that the Lphn2 and Lphn3 mutations do not impair surface transport of Lphn2 and Lphn3 or targeting to dendritic spines, but that the Lphn3 mutations abolish its ability to rescue the decrease in synapse formation induced by conditional KO of Lphn3.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of evidence, referring to data in Figure 3.

claim: Analysis of the in vivo activity of WT and mutant Lphn2 and Lphn3 using sparse postsynaptic deletions demonstrated that WT Lphn2 and Lphn3 restored only the loss of synaptic connectivity of their cognate synapses.
source: Third, analysis of the in vivo activity of WT and mutant Lphn2 and Lphn3 using sparse postsynaptic deletions of these molecules in hippocampal CA1 neurons in conditional KO mice demonstrated that WT Lphn2 and Lphn3 restored only the loss of synaptic connectivity of their cognate synapses, but had no effect on those synapses for which these latrophilins normally are not required.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of evidence, referring to data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: WT Lphn2 and Lphn3 had no effect on synapses for which these latrophilins normally are not required.
source: Third, analysis of the in vivo activity of WT and mutant Lphn2 and Lphn3 using sparse postsynaptic deletions of these molecules in hippocampal CA1 neurons in conditional KO mice demonstrated that WT Lphn2 and Lphn3 restored only the loss of synaptic connectivity of their cognate synapses, but had no effect on those synapses for which these latrophilins normally are not required.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of evidence, referring to data in Figures 4 and 5 showing input-specific effects.

claim: Mutant Lphn2 and Lphn3 that is unable to mediate GPCR signaling is incompetent to rescue the conditional KO phenotype in vivo.
source: More importantly, these experiments established that mutant Lphn2 and Lphn3 that is unable to mediate GPCR signaling is incompetent to rescue the conditional KO phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of evidence, referring to data in Figures 4-6.

claim: Lphn2 and Lphn3 function in synapse formation as GPCRs.
source: Together, these lines of evidence show that Lphn2 and Lphn3 function in synapse formation as GPCRs.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the Discussion, based on the combined evidence from all experiments.

claim: The present study does not identify the nature of the GPCR signal that is activated by latrophilins in synapse formation.
source: However, the present study has inherent limitations. Most importantly, our results do not identify the nature of the GPCR signal that is activated by latrophilins in synapse formation.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a limitation of the study in the Discussion.

claim: Latrophilins have been reported to increase or decrease cAMP levels in cells in a constitutive manner.
source: Latrophilins have been reported to increase or decrease cAMP levels in cells in a constitutive manner (Nazarko et al., 2018; Müller et al., 2015; Ovando-Zambrano et al., 2019; Scholz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The results support a function of latrophilins in increasing cAMP.
source: Our results support a function in increasing cAMP (Figure 2), but the physiological signaling activities of GPCRs are complex and what the precise type of signaling of latrophilins is in vivo may depend on the specific context.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The physiological signaling activities of GPCRs are complex and what the precise type of signaling of latrophilins is in vivo may depend on the specific context.
source: Our results support a function in increasing cAMP (Figure 2), but the physiological signaling activities of GPCRs are complex and what the precise type of signaling of latrophilins is in vivo may depend on the specific context.
evidence: This is a general statement about GPCR signaling complexity.

claim: The results establish that latrophilins act as GPCRs in synapse formation, but do not reveal what type of GPCR signaling drives synapse formation.
source: Although our results establish that latrophilins act as GPCRs in synapse formation, they do not reveal what type of GPCR signaling drives synapse formation.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a limitation in the Discussion.

claim: Pharmacological blockage of cAMP signaling impairs induction of spine synapses by glutamate.
source: The notion that this signaling may consist of increases in cAMP is attractive since pharmacological blockage of cAMP signaling impairs induction of spine synapses by glutamate (Kwon and Sabatini, 2011), but no other evidence currently shows that cAMP signaling – or any other GPCR signaling – mediates synapse formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by a citation to Kwon and Sabatini, 2011.

claim: No evidence currently shows that cAMP signaling – or any other GPCR signaling – mediates synapse formation.
source: The notion that this signaling may consist of increases in cAMP is attractive since pharmacological blockage of cAMP signaling impairs induction of spine synapses by glutamate (Kwon and Sabatini, 2011), but no other evidence currently shows that cAMP signaling – or any other GPCR signaling – mediates synapse formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of current knowledge in the field.

claim: The role of the cytoplasmic sequences of latrophilins remains unclear.
source: Moreover, the role of the cytoplasmic sequences of latrophilins remains unclear.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a limitation in the Discussion.

claim: The long cytoplasmic sequences of latrophilins contain multiple highly conserved regions, including a C-terminal PDZ-domain binding motif.
source: These long sequences contain multiple highly conserved regions, including a C-terminal PDZ-domain binding motif (Sugita et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by a citation to Sugita et al., 1998.

claim: It is tempting to speculate that the cytoplasmic sequences of latrophilins confer context specificity to the general GPCR activity of latrophilins by binding to specific interacting partners.
source: What the function of these sequences is remains uncharacterized, although it is tempting to speculate that these sequences confer context specificity to the general GPCR activity of latrophilins by binding to specific interacting partners.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation in the Discussion.

claim: SHANKs are prime candidates for interacting partners of latrophilins since they are postsynaptic scaffolding proteins that bind to latrophilins.
source: Such partners remain to be identified, although SHANKs are prime candidates since they are postsynaptic scaffolding proteins that bind to latrophilins (Kreienkamp et al., 2000; Tobaben et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to studies showing the interaction.

claim: Lphn2 and Lphn3 function as GPCRs in synapse formation, suggesting that compartmentalization of a canonical signaling pathway controlled by GPCRs may be instrumental in driving the assembly of synaptic connections into circuits and control their specificity.
source: In summary, we here establish that Lphn2 and Lphn3 function as GPCRs in synapse formation, suggesting the possibility that compartmentalization of a canonical signaling pathway widely used in biology and controlled by GPCRs may be instrumental in driving the assembly of synaptic connections into circuits and control their specificity.
evidence: This is the concluding statement of the Discussion, summarizing the main finding and its implications.

claim: The Lphn3-ECD mutant deletes all transmembrane regions and cytoplasmic sequences of Lphn3 and attaches its extracellular domains to the membrane using a GPI-anchor.
source: The Lphn3-ECD mutant deletes all transmembrane regions and cytoplasmic sequences of Lphn3 and attaches its extracellular domains to the membrane using a GPI-anchor, thereby preserving only the Lphn3 adhesion function and deleting all of its potential signaling capacity (Gokce and Südhof, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the design of mutants.

claim: The Lphn2-T4L and Lphn3-T4L mutants contain an insertion of a T4 lysozyme sequence into the 3rd intracellular loop of Lphn2 or Lphn3, which abolishes G-protein coupling and impairs arrestin signaling to these GPCRs.
source: The Lphn2-T4L and Lphn3-T4L mutants contain an insertion of a T4 lysozyme (T4L) sequence into the 3rd intracellular loop of Lphn2 or Lphn3, which abolishes G-protein coupling and impairs arrestin signaling to these GPCRs (Rosenbaum et al., 2007; Cherezov et al., 2007; Thorsen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the design of mutants and is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The Lphn3-ΔCt mutant truncates most of the cytoplasmic C-terminal sequences, thereby ablating cytoplasmic interactions.
source: The Lphn3-ΔCt mutant truncates most of the cytoplasmic C-terminal sequences, thereby ablating cytoplasmic interactions (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the design of mutants and is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The mutations had no effect on the surface transport of Lphn2 or Lphn3, nor did they impair the ability of Lphn2 or Lphn3 to form trans-cellular adhesion complexes with FLRT3 or Ten2.
source: The mutations had no effect on the surface transport of Lphn2 or Lphn3, nor did they impair the ability of Lphn2 or Lphn3 to form trans-cellular adhesion complexes with FLRT3 or Ten2, suggesting that the mutant latrophilins are folded and functional in protein-protein interactions (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data in Figure 1B showing cell aggregation assays.

claim: All Lphn2 and Lphn3 proteins were localized to the cell surface of neurons, with no apparent difference in localization between WT and mutant proteins.
source: All Lphn2 and Lphn3 proteins were localized to the cell surface of neurons, with no apparent difference in localization between WT and mutant proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The fixation procedure supports that the assay is sampling predominately surface FLAG-tagged protein in non-permeabilized conditions.
source: This control supports that our assay is sampling predominately surface FLAG-tagged protein in non-permeabilized conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by the control experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A potential problem of the cAMP measurements with pink Flamindo is the rather high background signal of pink Flamindo that is cAMP-independent.
source: A potential problem of the cAMP measurements with pink Flamindo is the rather high background signal of pink Flamindo that is cAMP-independent (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a limitation of the pink Flamindo indicator.

claim: The PKA-indicator construct has a much better signal-to-noise ratio than the fluorescent pink Flamindo indicator.
source: Immunocytochemical analysis of the PKA-indicator protein in HEK293T cells as a function of stimulation with forskolin and IBMX revealed a strong cAMP-dependent signal with a much better signal-to-noise ratio than the fluorescent pink Flamindo indicator (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: The fact that the input-output curves in the electrophysiological recordings are superimposable attests to the solidity of the findings and the validity of the approach for measuring synaptic connectivity.
source: The fact that the input-output curves in the electrophysiological recordings (Figures 4 and 5) are superimposable in these experiments attests to the solidity of the findings and the validity of the approach for measuring synaptic connectivity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an assessment of data quality.

claim: A decrease in synaptic strength might be due to other causes than a loss of synaptic connectivity.
source: However, a decrease in synaptic strength might be due to other causes than a loss of synaptic connectivity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a potential alternative interpretation.

claim: Quantitative retrograde monosynaptic rabies tracing allows in vivo analyses of synaptic connections formed by a specific postsynaptic neuron.
source: Quantitative retrograde monosynaptic rabies tracing allows in vivo analyses of synaptic connections formed by a specific postsynaptic neuron (Sando et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by a citation to a prior study.
